title: Adverse possession
subtitle: Factual possession, the 2002 Act scheme, and a fence dispute that changed the rules
objectives: Apply the Powell v McFarlane test for factual possession and intention to possess to a new fact pattern
Explain the Land Registration Act 2002 scheme for registered land, including the three conditions that can still give a squatter title after objection
Apply the corrected reading of the boundary condition (Sch 6, para 5(4)) following Brown v Ridley, and distinguish civil adverse possession from the criminal offence of residential squatting

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the classic test for factual possession — single and exclusive physical control of the land to the degree an occupying owner might be expected to exercise — plus the requisite intention to possess

leadingAuthorities.citation: JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2002] UKHL 30
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms intention to possess means intention to exclude the world at large, not necessarily an intention to own; adverse possession can defeat even a well-resourced registered paper owner

The registered land scheme: a squatter may apply for registration after ten years' adverse possession; if the paper owner objects, one of three conditions (including the boundary condition) can still give the squatter title
Creates the criminal offence of trespassing in a residential building with intent to live there — a separate, criminal-law overlay on the civil doctrine of adverse possession

Very recent Supreme Court authority holding the ten years of reasonable belief required by Sch 6, para 5(4) need not be the ten years immediately before the application — correcting the previously assumed reading, and current law that older materials likely misstate

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Adverse possession questions are almost always dressed up as a story — a fence, a shed, a strip of garden used for years without anyone objecting. Where the profile shows application is weaker than knowledge, this note appears: 'You know the ten-year scheme — this lesson is about reading a messy fact pattern and finding which condition, if any, actually fits.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the statutory scheme here before. This lesson leans on fact patterns — encroaching fences, disputed strips of garden, timing questions — so expect to apply the boundary condition, not just recite it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Take Parts 1 to 3 slowly before the Brown v Ridley material in Part 5 — you need the factual possession test and the three Sch 6 conditions solid first, or the correction won't make sense.

overview.hook: Your neighbour's fence has sat three feet over the boundary line for as long as anyone can remember. Nobody measured it when it went up; nobody complained. Then a survey happens — a sale, an inheritance, a falling-out — and suddenly everyone needs to know exactly whose land that three-foot strip is, and whether it's too late to get it back. This lesson follows that fence from 'nobody noticed' to 'the Supreme Court had to decide it in 2025' — because the rule you'd have learned even a couple of years ago just changed.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. This lesson reflects Brown v Ridley [2025] UKSC 7, decided by the Supreme Court in 2025, which corrected the widely assumed reading of the Sch 6, para 5(4) boundary condition under the Land Registration Act 2002. Materials predating this case will very likely state the older, now-incorrect assumption that the ten years of reasonable belief must be the ten years immediately before the application — treat Part 5 of this lesson as the current position.

parts.heading: The fence that moved
parts.voice: narrative, scenario-driven — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Picture a semi-detached house with a long back garden. Fifteen years ago, the previous owner put up a fence — but got it slightly wrong, enclosing a three-foot strip that, on the paper title, belongs to next door. Nobody measured it. The current owner has mown that strip, planted a hedge along it, stored a shed on it, and treated it as their own garden for the entire time they've lived there.

This is the everyday face of adverse possession: not a dramatic land grab, but an ordinary, unnoticed encroachment that hardens into a dispute only when someone finally checks. The law's starting question is deceptively simple — has the occupier had factual possession of the disputed strip, with the intention to possess it?

Powell v McFarlane supplies the classic test: factual possession requires a sufficient degree of physical control — exclusive to the occupier, and of the kind an occupying owner might be expected to exercise given the nature of the land — plus an intention to possess, meaning an intention to exercise that control for one's own benefit and to the exclusion of others, including the true owner. For an ordinary garden strip, mowing it, planting it, fencing it and using it as your own is usually more than enough evidence of both.

components.definition: A sufficient degree of exclusive physical control over land, of the kind an occupying owner might reasonably be expected to exercise given its nature — the first limb of the Powell v McFarlane test for adverse possession.

interaction.prompt: Name the two elements the Powell v McFarlane test requires for adverse possession, alongside the passage of the required time period.
acceptableAnswers: factual possession and intention to possess
factual possession and intention to possess (animus possidendi)
interaction.modelAnswer: Factual possession — sufficient, exclusive physical control of the land — and intention to possess (animus possidendi), the intention to exercise that control for oneself and exclude others, including the paper owner.

parts.heading: Intention to possess: what Pye actually decided
parts.voice: narrative, scenario-driven — continues the story with a real case
body: Back to the strip of garden — someone might object: 'they never intended to own that land, they just thought it was theirs already.' Surely that undermines any claim of intention to possess? JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham answers this directly, and the answer surprises most students on first read.

The Grahams farmed land under a grazing licence from Pye. The licence expired, Pye declined to renew it, and asked the Grahams to stop using the land — but never followed through, and the Grahams simply carried on farming it as before, for well over the twelve years then required. Pye argued the Grahams never intended to 'own' the land — they knew it wasn't theirs, and would have paid for a further licence if asked. The House of Lords rejected this. Intention to possess does not mean intention to acquire ownership; it means an intention to control the land and exclude everyone else, including the paper owner, for the time being.

This is why Pye is genuinely uncomfortable reading for a registered, well-resourced landowner: it confirms that even a company that clearly owns land on paper can lose it to someone who simply carries on using it, unchallenged, for long enough — because the law cares about what the occupier actually did with the land, not what they privately believed about legal title.

components.factsShort: Farmers continued grazing land under an expired licence for well over the required period, never challenged by the registered paper owner.
components.ratioShort: Intention to possess means intention to exclude the world at large from the land, not an intention to acquire ownership of it.

expanded.facts: The Grahams grazed land belonging to Pye under a succession of grazing agreements. The final agreement expired and Pye declined to renew it, briefly asking the Grahams to stop, then taking no further action. The Grahams continued to farm the land exactly as before for well over the limitation period. Pye, holding registered title, brought proceedings once it wished to develop the land, arguing the Grahams had never intended to possess it as owners.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords held that the relevant intention is an intention to possess, not an intention to own — an intention to occupy and control the land for one's own benefit, excluding other people so far as reasonably possible, including the paper owner. The Grahams' continued, exclusive farming of the land, unchallenged, satisfied both factual possession and intention to possess.
expanded.significance: Pye is the leading modern authority confirming adverse possession is available even against a solvent, registered corporate owner, and that a squatter's private awareness that the land legally belongs to someone else does not defeat the claim. It prompted the reforms now found in the Land Registration Act 2002, which make registered land harder (though not impossible) to lose this way.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows the Grahams had the requisite intention to possess, despite knowing the land legally belonged to Pye.
interaction.scenarioText: The Grahams' grazing licence expired. Pye asked them to stop using the land but took no further action. The Grahams continued to farm the land exactly as before, excluding anyone else from using it, for well over the required period, while privately accepting that Pye remained the paper owner.
tappableSpans: Pye asked them to stop using the land but took no further action
continued to farm the land exactly as before, excluding anyone else from using it
privately accepting that Pye remained the paper owner
interaction.correctSpan: continued to farm the land exactly as before, excluding anyone else from using it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Continuing to use and exclude others from the land is the conduct that shows intention to possess — Pye confirms this doesn't require believing you legally own it.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the ongoing conduct, not the private belief. Knowing the land 'really' belongs to someone else is irrelevant to intention to possess — what matters is continuing to occupy and exclude others.

parts.heading: The 2002 Act: applying after ten years
parts.voice: narrative, procedural — walks through the mechanics as a sequence of steps
body: For unregistered land, the old rule largely survives: twelve years of adverse possession extinguishes the paper owner's right to recover the land, full stop. Registered land is different and deliberately harder, because the whole point of registration is that the register — not who happens to be standing on the land — should tell you who owns it.

Under LRA 2002, Sch 6, an adverse possessor of registered land can apply to be registered as proprietor after just ten years (not twelve). But that application doesn't automatically succeed. The registrar must notify the paper owner, who can object. If the paper owner objects and does nothing further, the application is normally rejected outright — the scheme is designed to give a registered owner every opportunity to simply say no.

If the application is rejected, the squatter isn't necessarily finished. Three conditions in Sch 6, para 5 can still let them succeed: it would be unconscionable for the owner to object because of some equity by estoppel; the squatter is for some other reason entitled to the land (e.g. under a will that failed for some technical reason); or — the condition that matters most for our fence dispute — the land is adjacent to land already owned by the applicant, the exact boundary line has never been determined, and the applicant reasonably believed the disputed land belonged to them for at least ten years.

components.text: The third condition is that — (a) the land to which the application relates is adjacent to land belonging to the applicant, (b) the exact line of the boundary between the two has not been determined under rules under section 60, (c) for at least ten years of the period of adverse possession ending on the date of the application, the applicant (or any predecessor in title) reasonably believed that the land to which the application relates belonged to him, and (d) the estate to which the application relates was registered more than one year prior to the date of the application.
elements: The disputed land is adjacent to land already belonging to the applicant
The exact boundary line has never been formally determined
For at least ten years of the adverse possession, the applicant reasonably believed the land was theirs
The neighbouring registered estate was registered more than a year before the application

interaction.prompt: Under Sch 6, para 5(4), what must be true of the boundary between the two properties for the 'boundary condition' to be available at all?
options: The exact line of the boundary must never have been formally determined
The boundary must have been formally surveyed and fixed by the Land Registry
There must be no fence or hedge marking the boundary at all
interaction.explanation: The condition exists precisely for cases where nobody ever formally fixed the exact line — that's why an honest, long-standing mistake about where the boundary runs can qualify. A formally determined boundary takes the case outside this condition entirely.

parts.heading: A different kind of trespasser: the residential squatting offence
parts.voice: narrative, contrasting — pulls back from the fence story to a sharper example
body: Step away from the garden strip for a moment. Imagine instead someone breaks into an empty residential house and moves in, intending to live there. This looks superficially similar to adverse possession — occupying someone else's land without permission — but since 2012 it engages a completely different area of law.

LASPO 2012, s 144 created a criminal offence: trespassing in a residential building, with knowledge (or the means of knowledge) that you are a trespasser, and intending to live there even for a short period. This is squarely criminal law, prosecuted by the state, and separate from the civil question of whether ten or twelve years' possession might one day give someone title.

The two regimes can coexist uneasily on the same facts, but they answer different questions. The criminal offence is about the act of trespassing into a home with intent to reside; it doesn't itself extinguish anyone's civil title, and a squatter can be criminally liable under s 144 on day one, long before any civil adverse possession claim could even begin to run. Don't let a residential squatting fact pattern pull you into an adverse possession answer, or vice versa — check what the question is actually asking about.

components.label: Civil adverse possession vs criminal residential squatting
points: Adverse possession (civil): requires factual possession plus intention to possess, sustained for the statutory period (10 years registered, 12 years unregistered), and can apply to any land
Residential squatting offence (LASPO 2012, s 144): a criminal offence committed the moment someone trespasses in a residential building intending to live there, with no minimum time period at all
The offence does not extinguish the true owner's civil title, and a long-running civil adverse possession claim does not itself excuse the criminal offence at its outset
A fact pattern involving an occupied or recently occupied home is far more likely to raise the s 144 offence than a classic adverse possession claim

interaction.prompt: Put these in the order they would occur in a residential squatting scenario that could engage s 144 LASPO 2012.
items: A person enters an empty residential building as a trespasser
They know, or have reason to know, they are trespassing
They intend to live in the building, even briefly
The criminal offence under s 144 is complete, regardless of how long they go on to occupy it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the offence is complete almost immediately on entry with the relevant knowledge and intention. There is no waiting period, unlike the years required for a civil adverse possession claim.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — knowledge of trespassing and intention to live there are what complete the offence, and they can both be present from the moment of entry. No lapse of years is required.

parts.heading: Brown v Ridley: the fence story ends differently than you'd think
parts.voice: narrative, building to a genuine 'what you thought you knew has changed' moment
body: Back to that three-foot strip of garden. Suppose the current owner reasonably believed, for a solid stretch of years, that the strip was theirs — but a boundary dispute later flared up (a new neighbour, a survey, an argument) several years before they finally got round to applying under Sch 6. By the date of the application, they no longer reasonably believe the land is theirs — the dispute has told them otherwise.

Read Sch 6, para 5(4)(c) quickly, and you'll likely assume — as most lawyers did before 2025 — that the 'at least ten years... ending on the date of the application' language means the ten years of reasonable belief has to run right up to the application itself. On that reading, our fence-owner is out of luck: their belief stopped being reasonable once the dispute started, so there's no unbroken run of ten years' belief ending on the application date.

Brown v Ridley says that reading is wrong. The Supreme Court held in 2025 that the ten years of reasonable belief required by para 5(4)(c) do not have to be the ten years immediately preceding the application — an earlier ten-year period of reasonable belief, at some point during the overall period of adverse possession, can satisfy the condition, even if that belief later ceased (for example, because a dispute arose) before the application was actually made.

This is a genuine doctrinal shift, not a minor clarification, and it changes outcomes: an occupier who reasonably believed the land was theirs for a solid ten-year stretch, but then had that belief disturbed by a later dispute, is not automatically shut out of the boundary condition just because their belief wasn't still 'live' at the moment they applied. If your notes, a textbook, or a past exam answer state that the relevant ten years must immediately precede the application, they are stating the pre-2025 assumption — Brown v Ridley has corrected it, and this is now the law you should apply.

components.commonWrongAnswer: The ten years of reasonable belief under Sch 6, para 5(4)(c) must be the ten years immediately before the date of the application — if belief lapsed earlier because of a dispute, the boundary condition is unavailable.
components.whyItsWrong: This was the widely assumed reading before Brown v Ridley [2025] UKSC 7, but the Supreme Court has now held it is incorrect. Any ten-year period of reasonable belief occurring during the period of adverse possession can satisfy the condition — it need not be the period running up to the application itself, even if the applicant's belief had since been disturbed.

interaction.prompt: Applying Brown v Ridley [2025] UKSC 7, which applicant can still satisfy the para 5(4)(c) reasonable-belief condition?
interaction.scenarioA: An applicant reasonably believed a disputed strip was theirs from years 1 to 11 of their occupation, but a boundary dispute arose in year 12, three years before they applied in year 15 — by the time of the application their belief was no longer reasonable.
interaction.scenarioB: An applicant has never at any point believed the disputed strip was theirs — they knew from the outset it belonged to their neighbour, but occupied it anyway.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A has an unbroken ten-year run of reasonable belief (years 1–11) at some point during the adverse possession, which Brown v Ridley confirms is enough even though that belief had lapsed by the time of the application in year 15. B never had reasonable belief at any point, so no version of the condition — old or new reading — helps them.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on whether there is any unbroken ten-year stretch of reasonable belief during the period of adverse possession, not on whether belief was still held at the date of application — that's exactly what Brown v Ridley changed. An applicant who never believed the land was theirs at any point still fails regardless.

testPool.prompt: Name the two elements required by the Powell v McFarlane test for adverse possession.
acceptableAnswers: factual possession and intention to possess
testPool.modelAnswer: Factual possession (sufficient, exclusive physical control appropriate to the land) and intention to possess (an intention to exercise that control for oneself, excluding others including the paper owner).

testPool.prompt: How many years of adverse possession are generally required before a squatter of unregistered land can extinguish the paper owner's right to recover it?
options: Twelve years
Ten years
Six years

testPool.prompt: What did JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham decide about intention to possess?
options: It means an intention to control the land and exclude others, including the paper owner — not an intention to acquire ownership of it
It means the occupier must genuinely believe they already own the land
It means the occupier must intend to eventually pay the paper owner for the land
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often assume intention to possess requires believing you own the land, or planning to formalise ownership somehow. Pye rejects both — the Grahams knew Pye was the paper owner and still succeeded, because what mattered was their conduct excluding others.

testPool.prompt: Under the LRA 2002 Sch 6 scheme for registered land, what happens if the paper owner objects to a squatter's application after ten years and takes no further steps?
options: The application is normally rejected, unless one of the three Sch 6 conditions is satisfied
The application always succeeds regardless of the objection
The paper owner automatically loses title the moment they fail to respond within 24 hours

testPool.prompt: Put the stages of a registered-land adverse possession application in order.
items: Squatter completes ten years of adverse possession
Squatter applies under Sch 6 to be registered as proprietor
Registrar notifies the paper owner, who may object
If rejected, the squatter may still succeed by satisfying one of the three Sch 6 conditions

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that best supports factual possession of the disputed strip of garden.
testPool.scenarioText: The current owner moved into the house eleven years ago. They occasionally noticed the fence seemed to run further than expected, mowed the whole enclosed area including the disputed strip every week, and once mentioned to a friend that they weren't entirely sure where the legal boundary was.
tappableSpans: occasionally noticed the fence seemed to run further than expected
mowed the whole enclosed area including the disputed strip every week
once mentioned to a friend that they weren't entirely sure where the legal boundary was
testPool.correctSpan: mowed the whole enclosed area including the disputed strip every week
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — regular, exclusive physical use of the land (mowing, maintaining it as garden) is the clearest evidence of factual possession. Private doubts about the legal boundary don't undermine that, per Pye.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on physical conduct over the land, not private thoughts or noticing. Weekly mowing of the whole enclosed strip is the strongest evidence of the exclusive physical control Powell v McFarlane requires.

options: Trespassing in a residential building, knowing or having reason to know you are a trespasser, and intending to live there
Any unauthorised use of another person's land, residential or otherwise
Failing to leave commercial premises after a landlord terminates a lease

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is governed by the LASPO 2012, s 144 criminal offence, rather than the civil law of adverse possession?
testPool.scenarioA: Someone breaks into an empty house last week, knowing it isn't theirs, and starts sleeping there.
testPool.scenarioB: A homeowner has mown and fenced a disputed garden strip belonging on paper to their neighbour for the last eleven years, without incident.
testPool.explanation: A is a fresh trespass into a residential building with intent to live there — exactly what s 144 criminalises, with no waiting period. B is the classic slow-building civil adverse possession scenario, engaging Sch 6 rather than any criminal offence.

testPool.prompt: An applicant reasonably believed a disputed strip of land was theirs for years 2 to 12 of an eighteen-year period of occupation, but a formal boundary dispute in year 14 destroyed that belief before they applied in year 18. Applying Brown v Ridley, can the para 5(4)(c) condition still be satisfied?
options: Yes — an earlier unbroken ten-year period of reasonable belief during the adverse possession is enough, even though belief had lapsed by the date of application
No — the ten years of reasonable belief must run immediately up to the date of the application
No — once any dispute arises, the entire application fails regardless of when the dispute occurred
testPool.explanation: This is exactly the fact pattern Brown v Ridley resolved: years 2–12 give an unbroken ten-year run of reasonable belief, and the Supreme Court held that period need not be the one ending on the application date.

testPool.prompt: What was the widely assumed (and now corrected) reading of Sch 6, para 5(4)(c) before Brown v Ridley?
options: That the ten years of reasonable belief had to be the ten years immediately preceding the date of the application
That reasonable belief was never required at all under the boundary condition
That the boundary condition only applied to commercial land
testPool.trapExplanation: The pre-2025 assumption read the statutory phrase 'ending on the date of the application' as requiring an unbroken run of belief right up to the application. Brown v Ridley held this reading was wrong — any qualifying ten-year period during the adverse possession can suffice.

testPool.prompt: Which Supreme Court case corrected the reading of the ten-year reasonable-belief requirement in Sch 6, para 5(4)?
options: Brown v Ridley [2025] UKSC 7
JA Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2002] UKHL 30
Powell v McFarlane (1977) 38 P & CR 452

testPool.prompt: Tomasz has occupied a disputed strip of his neighbour's registered garden for fourteen years, mowing and planting it throughout. He reasonably believed it was his own land for the first ten years, but a survey in year 11 revealed the true boundary, after which he continued using the strip anyway, now knowing it wasn't his. He applies under Sch 6 in year 14. Analyse whether the para 5(4)(c) condition can be satisfied.
factsToOrder: Tomasz occupies and maintains the strip for fourteen years
He reasonably believed the strip was his for years 1 to 10
A survey in year 11 reveals the true boundary, ending his reasonable belief
He applies for registration in year 14, after continuing to occupy despite knowing the truth

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC shown, mapping each fact to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student identifies the Issue, drags facts into Application, writes the Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Tomasz can satisfy the reasonable-belief requirement in Sch 6, para 5(4)(c), given his belief lapsed four years before he applied.
modelAnswer.rule: Para 5(4)(c) requires at least ten years of reasonable belief that the land belonged to the applicant. Following Brown v Ridley [2025] UKSC 7, this ten-year period need not be the period immediately preceding the application — an earlier qualifying ten-year period during the overall adverse possession is sufficient, even if belief later ceased.
modelAnswer.application: Tomasz's reasonable belief ran unbroken from year 1 to year 10 — exactly ten years. That the survey in year 11 destroyed his belief before he applied in year 14 would previously have been assumed fatal, but Brown v Ridley confirms it is not: the qualifying ten-year period occurred, and that is enough, regardless of the gap before application.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Tomasz can satisfy the para 5(4)(c) condition, provided the other elements (adjacency, undetermined boundary, prior registration timing) are also met, applying the corrected post-Brown v Ridley reading.

testPool.prompt: A squatter occupies unregistered land for thirteen years, with clear factual possession and intention to possess throughout, and no objection is ever raised by the paper owner. What is the effect?
options: The paper owner's right to recover the land is extinguished after twelve years — the squatter's possession is effectively unchallengeable
Nothing changes until the squatter formally applies to the Land Registry, as with registered land
The squatter commits a criminal offence the moment the twelve-year period is reached
testPool.explanation: Unregistered land follows the older limitation-based rule: twelve years' adverse possession extinguishes the paper owner's right to recover the land automatically, without any Sch 6-style application process.

testPool.prompt: Does a long-running civil adverse possession claim excuse someone from criminal liability under LASPO 2012, s 144 if they initially entered a residential building as a trespasser intending to live there?
options: No — the criminal offence is complete at the point of entry with the relevant knowledge and intention, independent of any later civil possession claim
Yes — once ten years have passed, the criminal offence is automatically extinguished

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's items is assuming the ten years of reasonable belief under Sch 6, para 5(4)(c) must run right up to the date of the application. Brown v Ridley corrected this in 2025 — any qualifying ten-year period during the adverse possession can be enough, even if belief later lapsed.
